Our answers to TelAgri’s twelve Week 1 prompts

TelAgri provided twelve independent investigation prompts for Week 1, in three themes. This report is our response. Each card below shows TelAgri’s prompt exactly as provided, a short answer taken from the author’s own text, and a link to the full answer with its tables, equations, figures and citations.

Theme A Yield-loss drivers and bloom · Pablo Orozco Quesada · Orestis Giannopoulos

A1Pablo Orozco Quesada · Orestis Giannopoulos

What are the most important drivers of blueberry yield loss, at which growth stages do they matter most, and which can we measure from public data?

Our answer in brief

Eight drivers matter: winter chill shortfall, spring frost, pollination weather, reproductive heat, summer heat and drought, excess rain and humidity, hail and wind, and crop load and pruning. Frost peaks at open bloom and young fruit; pollination only matters during the short bloom window. Weather-driven drivers are measurable from public data; crop state (bud load, cultivar, management) is not.

Read the full answer →
A2Pablo Orozco Quesada · Orestis Giannopoulos

What simple deterministic structure could translate a weather or stress event into expected loss—for example, intensity x duration x phenology-stage sensitivity?

Our answer in brief

Exposure = degree-hours past a stage-specific threshold (intensity × duration). A saturating damage curve per stage converts exposure into the fraction of flowers or fruit lost, weighted by the share of flowers in each stage. That fraction reduces one yield component; losses multiply through the season instead of adding.

Read the full answer →
A3Pablo Orozco Quesada · Orestis Giannopoulos

How should we predict bloom timing and bloom progression for our use case? Compare a basic ChillR approach with alternatives such as a chill-forcing model, PhenoFlex, or a locally calibrated temperature model.

Our answer in brief

Use chillR to compute Chill Portions and GDH, and build a sequential chill → forcing model with priors by cultivar group, benchmarked against heat-only. Model progression as a distribution of heat requirements (10/50/90% bloom). PhenoFlex has 12 parameters and needs 15–20+ seasons, so it is a later challenger, not a starting point.

Read the full answer →
A4Pablo Orozco Quesada · Orestis Giannopoulos

What data would we need to calibrate or validate a bloom and yield-loss model later, and what can we use immediately without field observations?

Our answer in brief

Now: ERA5-Land hourly weather, station records, terrain and night LST, satellite imagery, literature priors, national statistics. Later: block registry, BBCH phenology, canopy temperature loggers, bud counts and fruit set, post-frost damage assessments, harvest records, and any historical block yields. The 2027 bloom is the first calibration window.

Read the full answer →

Berry enlargement should receive the highest initial physiological priority for current-season water-stress effects.

Keep canopy potential, water deficit, previous-season condition, and chlorophyll separate until their independent predictive value is demonstrated.

Theme C Satellite indices, weeds and flooding · Giannis Gallios · G for Geoscience

C1Giannis Gallios

How should we measure NDRE, NDMI, NDVI, fapar, and Cab for blueberry blocks if we know that they are strongly tied to yield? How do we contextualize those values or make them meaningful?

Our answer in brief

For each confirmed block, extract a quality-controlled seasonal time series, then compare the same location with its own earlier observations and with similar blocks at the same stage. … Their values describe spectral properties of the vegetation–soil mixture; field records explain what caused a change.

Read the full answer →
C2Giannis Gallios

What satellite-based approach could identify flooding, persistent wetness, or likely anaerobic root-zone conditions? Are there indices that you are comfortable with that can distinguish surface inundation (or even persistent saturation) that can be detected? What are the limitations of that approach?

Our answer in brief

Begin with a regional view that requires little local data, then add event observations and field checks. … Satellites can sometimes detect exposed water; repeat observations cannot show continuous saturation between passes. … A susceptibility score is a relative screening layer, not a calibrated flood probability.

Read the full answer →
C3Giannis Gallios

How could we rate weed control in a blueberry orchard using remote sensing? What is feasible with Sentinel-2 at 10 m, and when would higher-resolution drone or aerial imagery be necessary?

Our answer in brief

Use Sentinel-2 for broad vegetation context, test Planet where zones span multiple pixels, and use drone or aerial imagery for individual rows and small patches. … This visual test demonstrates spatial detail, not validated weed detection.

Read the full answer →
C4Giannis Gallios

Our answer in brief

Begin with a few complementary feature groups rather than treating every index as an independent yield driver. … Departure severity × affected fraction × persistence gives a relative inspection priority.

How the answers connect

Three themes, one shared yield model

Theme A · Phenology & eventsWhen is the crop exposed, and to what?Bloom model gives the daily share of flowers in each stage, p(k, t); each weather event damages one yield component, and losses multiply through the season.
Theme B · Water limitationHow limited is water, stage by stage?Root-zone water balance → stage-specific water-deficit score Ds for bloom, fruit set, berry enlargement and ripening, kept separate from canopy and chlorophyll indicators.
Theme C · Satellite evidenceWhere and when does the canopy change?Quality-controlled index time series per confirmed block; departure severity × affected fraction × persistence → inspection priority.
Common thread across the three themes: all numbers are starting points, not calibrated values. Theme A: “Every number below is a literature prior, not a Georgian calibration.” Theme B: “Convert water-deficit scores to yield impacts only after validation with observed yield, berry weight, or plant-water-status data.” Theme C: “Yield-loss percentages require a later relationship with field yield records.” Confirmed blocks, phenology and yield records from TelAgri are the shared next requirement — see our questions for TelAgri.
Theme A · TelAgri prompts A1–A4

Yield-loss drivers and bloom

Answered by Pablo Orozco Quesada · Orestis Giannopoulos · Session 1 briefing · Blueberry modeling, Georgia · October 2026

Our working position: predict the phenological stage first, then let each weather event damage one yield component, and propagate those losses sequentially to yield. Every number below is a literature prior, not a Georgian calibration. This briefing supports the Session 1 deck and is meant to be tested against Telagri’s current model and data.

The yield identity behind all four answers (Strik et al. 2017, with a survival term added for stress modeling):

Yield identity Y=Nbud×Fbud×FS×Spreharvest×Wberry

N(bud) is flower buds per plant, F(bud) flowers per bud, FS fruit set (0–1), S(preharvest) the share of set fruit surviving to harvest, and W(berry) mean berry mass.

A1 · Drivers, stages, measurability

Yield-loss drivers, sensitive stages and measurability

TelAgri prompt A1

What are the most important drivers of blueberry yield loss, at which growth stages do they matter most, and which can we measure from public data?

Eight drivers explain most weather- and management-related blueberry yield loss; each acts in its own stage window and on a specific yield component. Temperature-driven drivers can be computed from public hourly weather today; crop state cannot.

When each driver matters

Sensitivity = how strongly the stage responds if the event happens, not how likely the event is. Frequency is site-specific and comes from the weather analysis.

DriverDormancyBud swell → pink budBloomPetal fall, young fruitBerry growth, ripeningPost-harvest (bud initiation)
Winter chill shortfallHighMedMed———
Spring frost / freezeLowMedHighHigh——
Poor pollination weather——High———
Reproductive heat—HighMed———
Summer heat and drought———LowHighMed
Excess rain, humidity——MedLowHigh—
Hail, strong wind——LowMedMed—
Crop load, pruningMed———HighMed

Why these ratings:

  • Chill acts in winter but shows up later: insufficient chill gives delayed or uneven budbreak, extended flowering, weak leafing and lower reproductive performance.
  • Frost tolerance collapses as buds open: dormant highbush buds survive −29 to −34 °C, while open flowers and young fruit are damaged within minutes at about −2.8 and −2.2 °C.
  • Pollination matters only during bloom: each flower is receptive for roughly 3–5 days, and rain, cold, wind and humidity cut bee flight and pollen release.
  • Reproductive heat: 37.5 °C for 4 h was most damaging at bud swell in ‘Bluecrop’ (39% lower fruit set).
  • Summer heat, drought and rain act on berry mass, fruit survival and the marketable fraction; post-harvest stress can reduce next season’s flower buds.
  • Crop load and pruning set flower-bud number and compete for carbon with berry growth.

What each driver damages and whether public data can see it

DriverYield component modifiedPublic-data proxyMeasurable?
Winter chill shortfallBloom timing and spread; flowers per budHourly temperature → Chill Portions (ERA5-Land)Yes
Spring frostFlower survival; young-fruit survivalHourly temperature × modeled stage; night land-surface temperature and terrain for cold pocketsYes, with bias correction
Pollination weatherFruit set; seed set → berry massBee-flight hours (temperature, rain, wind) inside the bloom windowPartly (no bee or hive data)
Reproductive heatFruit setHours above ~35 °C at bud swell and bloomYes
Summer heat, droughtBerry mass; next year’s budsTemperature, VPD, rainfall, ET₀; canopy indices (Sentinel-2)Partly (irrigation unknown)
Excess rain, humidityFruit survival; marketable fractionRainfall, humidity, wet-hour counts at bloom and harvestPartly (disease pressure unknown)
Hail, strong windFlower and fruit survivalConvective proxies; severe-weather reportsWeak
Crop load, pruningFlower buds; berry massNot public; canopy vigor at mostNo
Gridded air temperature is not bud temperature. Frost and heat exposure need a station or canopy-logger check before calibration, especially for night minima in valleys.

Priorities for western Georgia (hypotheses)

These are bets to test against Telagri’s loss records, not conclusions. Their order depends on cultivar mix, site and protection (tunnels, nets, frost control).

  1. Frost after early warm spells. Low-chill (southern highbush) cultivars can break bud early in mild winters; a later cold night then hits open flowers. First test: back-cast frost exposure by stage; ask growers which years had damage.
  2. Wet, cool bloom limits fruit set. Western Georgia receives very high rainfall; rain and cool hours stop bee flight, humidity cuts pollen release and favors blossom blight. First test: bee-flight hours during bloom against yield history.
  3. Chill shortfall for higher-chill cultivars. Mild Black Sea winters may not satisfy northern highbush cultivars such as Duke or Bluecrop every year. First test: Chill Portions climatology by site against cultivar priors.
  4. Rain at ripening. Fruit rot, cracking and harvest delays reduce marketable yield. First test: rain and humidity in the harvest window against packout.
  5. Summer heat spells. Smaller, softer berries and a possible effect on next year’s flower buds. First test: hot hours during berry growth against berry weight.
The cultivar list in commercial Georgian farms (Legacy, Suziblue, Blue Ribbon, Duke, Bluecrop, Top Shelf and others) mixes low-chill and higher-chill types, so timing risks can run in opposite directions within one farm.

A2 · Event → expected loss

From a weather event to expected loss

TelAgri prompt A2

What simple deterministic structure could translate a weather or stress event into expected loss—for example, intensity x duration x phenology-stage sensitivity?

A simple deterministic structure: stage sensitivity filters an exposure that combines intensity and duration; a saturating damage curve turns that exposure into the fraction of one yield component lost; losses then propagate sequentially.

Each stage needs only two parameters (a threshold and a steepness), which can be set from literature now and refitted with Georgian data later.

The chain

01 · StageStage shareThe bloom model gives p(k, t), the share of flowers in stage k on day t.
02 · ExposureDegree-hoursHourly temperature beyond the stage-specific threshold, in degree-hours.
03 · DamageSaturating curveA saturating curve per stage (and later per cultivar) converts exposure into a fraction lost.
04 · ComponentState updateThat fraction reduces the state it acts on — flowers, fruit set, fruit survival or berry mass.
05 · YieldAt harvestYield emerges at harvest from the updated states.

Equations

Frost exposure for stage k (heat mirrors it above an upper threshold):

Exposure Ek=∑tmax(0,Tcrit,k−Tt)Δt

Damage fraction (a logistic fitted to LT10/LT50/LT90 is an equivalent option):

Damage fraction Dk=1−e−βkEk

Stage-weighted damage and the state update:

Stage-weighted damage · state update D=∑kpk(t)DkNafter=Nbefore(1−D)
Why this beats “Tmin below X = Y% loss”: −3 °C for 10 minutes and −3 °C for 4 hours no longer look identical; −6 °C and −3 °C are separated by severity; and the threshold moves every day as the phenology advances.

Which component each event modifies

Event and timingPrimary biological targetComponent modified
Frost on expanding budsFloral primordia, flowersPotential flower number
Frost at bloomPistil, ovaryFlower survival / fruit set
Frost just after bloomYoung fruitFruit survival
Heat at bud swellDeveloping pollenFruit set
Heat at bloomPollen tube vs ovule windowFruit set
Poor pollination weatherPollen delivery, seed setFruit set and berry mass
Heat or drought in fruit growthPhotosynthesis, water and carbon balanceBerry mass / fruit survival
Rain at ripeningRot, cracking, harvest lossSurvival / marketable fraction

Combining events: multiply, do not add

Later stresses act only on what earlier stresses left. Illustrative numbers, not Georgian estimates:

StepMultiplierRelative yield
Potential—1.000
Frost at bloom kills 20% of flowers× 0.800.800
Wet bloom lowers fruit set of survivors by 10%× 0.900.720
Heat spell lowers berry mass by 5%× 0.950.684

The sequential model gives a 31.6% loss with each event attributed; adding percentages gives 35% and double-counts flowers already lost. With many events in a season, summed percentages can exceed 100%. Blueberry can partly compensate for fewer fruit with heavier berries; a compensation term can be added once data can size it, and stays off until then.

Starting priors from the literature

Module and stagePriorSourceCaveat
Frost, dormant flower budHighbush survives −29 to −34 °C; rabbiteye often damaged below −18 °CNC State ExtensionSouthern highbush less hardy
Frost, bud swellExposed flowers start to die below −6.7 °CNC State ExtensionUS conditions
Frost, corolla half outWhole flowers killed at −3.9 to −3.3 °CNC State ExtensionStage definitions vary
Frost, open bloom−2.8 °C for more than a few minutesNC State ExtensionDuration-sensitive
Frost, after corolla dropA few minutes below −2.2 °C; most sensitive stageNC State ExtensionDuration-sensitive
Heat, bud swell37.5 °C for 4 h → 39% lower fruit set (‘Bluecrop’)Scientific Reports (2025)One cultivar, controlled
Heat, bloomNo pollen-tube gain above 30 °C; faster ovule degeneration (‘Brightwell’)Yang et al. 2019, JASHSOne cultivar, controlled
Pollination, bloomFlowers receptive ~3–5 days; cross-pollen raised fruit mass 42% on average in 9 of 10 southern highbush cultivarsOSU Extension; UF/IFAS (Larue et al. 2025)Cultivar-specific
Honest output before calibration: until these are calibrated on Georgian cultivars and microclimates, the honest output is a risk class (low, moderate, high) with the expected loss range behind it, not a single precise percentage. A visual corolla-browning score can overstate or misrepresent the eventual fruit-set loss, so damage curves should be fitted to flower or fruit survival, not to appearance.

A3 · Bloom timing and progression

Predicting bloom timing and bloom progression

TelAgri prompt A3

How should we predict bloom timing and bloom progression for our use case? Compare a basic ChillR approach with alternatives such as a chill-forcing model, PhenoFlex, or a locally calibrated temperature model.

Recommendation: start with a sequential chill → forcing model (Chill Portions to a cultivar chill requirement, then growing degree hours to each stage threshold), built with chillR functions and literature priors by cultivar group, and always benchmarked against a heat-only model. Treat bloom as a distribution, not a date. PhenoFlex is a later challenger once there are 15–20+ seasons of observations.

chillR is a toolbox, not a model

A “basic chillR approach” usually means computing chill and heat metrics (Chill Hours, Utah units, Chill Portions, GDH) from hourly temperature. chillR also hosts the advanced options (PLS window analysis, PhenoFlex). The real choice is model structure against the data available.

ApproachHow it worksParametersData to calibrateRole for us
Heat-only (GDD/GDH)Heat from a fixed start date to a stage threshold2–3A few seasons of bloom datesBenchmark any model must beat
chillR, basic useChill Hours, Utah units, Chill Portions and GDH as indicesnoneNoneClimatologies now
Sequential chill → forcingChill Portions up to CR, then GDH up to each stage threshold3–4 per cultivar2+ seasons, several sitesCore engine now, with priors
Locally calibrated temperature modelEmpirical fit of local bloom dates to temperature2–5Many local yearsGood inside the observed range, weak transfer
PLS window analysis (chillR)Finds chill and forcing periods from long recordsstatisticalDecades of bloom datesNot feasible yet
PhenoFlex (chillR)Dynamic Model + GDH, joined by a sigmoid chill–heat transition1215–20+ seasons recommendedLater challenger

Why the Dynamic Model for chill: it treats chilling as a two-step process in which warm spells can undo uncommitted chill, which suits mild, fluctuating Black Sea winters. Utah-type models can give implausible or negative totals in warm climates, and Chill Hours handle warm interruptions poorly. Chill requirements are not convertible between metrics: 500 Chill Hours is not proportional to any fixed number of Chill Portions across sites.

Staged pathway

StageModelWhat we do
Now
No field data		Sequential Chill Portions → GDHPriors by cultivar group (low-chill vs higher-chill); ERA5-Land hourly checked against stations; output a stage distribution with an uncertainty band from parameter ranges; heat-only benchmark
Seasons 1–2
of observations		Locally calibrated sequential modelFit CR, base temperature and stage thresholds per main cultivar on BBCH scores; validate by leaving whole sites or years out; test whether chill adds skill over heat-only
15+ site-seasons
per cultivar		Challengers (PhenoFlex, overlap models)Adopt only if they lower out-of-sample error; then run climate scenarios
Decision rule: a model replaces a simpler one only if it lowers held-out error (RMSE and bias, in days) across years and sites. Supporting evidence: with 22 years of ‘Duke’ data in New Jersey, models combining chill and GDD beat single-variable models, with cross-validated R² above 0.85 for peak truss stage and above 0.75 for bloom onset (Shope et al. 2026, a preprint).

Bloom progression: a distribution of heat requirements

Buds on a bush, bushes in a block and canopy positions differ in their heat requirement. The simplest deterministic representation gives each block a mean and a spread:

Share of flowers open F(t)=Φ(H(t)−μσ)

F(t) is the share of flowers open; H(t) is forcing (GDH) accumulated since the chill requirement was met; μ is the forcing needed for 50% bloom; σ is the spread. Flowers that open on a given day stay receptive for about 3–5 days, which yields the daily share in each stage, p(k, t), used in the Q2 damage equation (A2).

Outputs per block: 10%, 50% and 90% bloom dates, bloom duration, and the daily stage shares feeding the frost, heat and pollination modules. Stage definitions should follow the blueberry BBCH scale (Wichura et al. 2024) so field scores and model output mean the same thing, and flower-bud and leaf-bud phenology should be kept separate.

A4 · Data now and later

Data: what we can use now and what we need later

TelAgri prompt A4

What data would we need to calibrate or validate a bloom and yield-loss model later, and what can we use immediately without field observations?

The weather side of the model can be built today from public data; calibration and validation need block-level observations, and each module needs its own. The 2027 bloom is the first chance to collect them, so the protocol has to be in place before bud swell.

Usable immediately, without field observations

SourceWhat it givesUse in the model
ERA5-Land (Copernicus)Hourly temperature, dew point, wind, rain; 0.1° (~9 km); 1950 onwardChill, forcing, frost and heat exposure; climatologies
Weather stations (NOAA ISD/GHCN; national network on request)Point hourly or daily recordsBias-check the reanalysis, especially night minima
MODIS night land-surface temperature, Copernicus DEM, SoilGrids1 km surface temperature; 30 m terrain; soil pH and textureFlag frost-prone blocks (cold-air pooling); site context
Sentinel-2, Landsat, Sentinel-1Optical imagery at 10–30 m; radar that sees through cloudMap blocks, canopy vigor and anomalies
Published priors (Extension, peer-reviewed)Critical temperatures, chill and heat ranges, heat and pollination effectsDefault parameters, graded by evidence
FAOSTAT, Geostat, trade data; grower variety listsNational area, output, exports; cultivars presentTrend sanity check only; cultivar groups to parameterize

What this alone can deliver: chill and frost-risk maps by district, back-casts of seasons growers remember as bad, and a sensitivity analysis showing which parameters move the output most — which tells us what to measure first. National statistics cannot validate a block-level model.

Needed to calibrate and validate

DataMinimum protocolConstrains
Block registryCultivar, planting year, density, tunnels or nets, frost protection, hives per haEvery module
PhenologyWeekly BBCH scores from bud swell to petal fall; % open flowers on tagged shoots; main cultivars at 3+ sitesChill requirement, heat thresholds, bloom spread
Canopy temperatureHourly loggers in a subset of blocks across elevation and terrainFrost and heat exposure; reanalysis bias
Bud load and fruit setDormant flower-bud counts and flowers per bud; tagged clusters counted after bloomPotential yield; pollination and bloom-stress functions
Event damageCut buds and flowers 24–72 h after a frost or heat event; % dead pistils by stageDamage curves (Tcrit, β)
HarvestBlock kg by pick; berry-weight subsamples; packoutBerry mass; final validation
HistoryMulti-year block yields and remembered frost, heat or rain eventsBack-cast validation, usable immediately if it exists
Validation rules:
  • Calibrate each module on the observations that inform it, not everything on final yield: the same yield can come from many small berries or fewer large ones.
  • Hold out whole years or sites for validation.
  • Score phenology in days (RMSE, bias) and losses by component, and only then check final yield as an integration test.
  • Define the yield target before validating: biological, harvested and marketable yield are not interchangeable.

B1Water stress by growth stage and stage weightsB2Estimating water stress without block-scale ETaB3A practical water-balance / ET-deficit scoreB4Productivity indicator without double countingReferencesTheme B references
B1 · Water stress by growth stage

Water stress across blueberry growth stages

TelAgri prompt B1

How does water stress affect blueberry yield at different stages—bloom, fruit set, berry enlargement, ripening, and post-harvest—and which periods should receive the highest weight?

The effect of water stress on blueberry productivity depends on phenological stage, stress severity and duration, cultivar, and environmental conditions. For modeling purposes, the main effects should be separated into fruit number, berry mass, quality, and next-season reproductive potential.

Bloom and fruit set. Water stress during bloom can reduce reproductive success by affecting floral function, nectar production, pollinator activity, and fruit set. In ‘Bluecrop’ and ‘Duke’, moderate deficit from floral bud break through flowering reduced nectar production, pollinator visitation, and fruit set (Castro et al., 2026). Stress during fruit set and early berry development may further restrict fruit establishment, cell division, turgor, and carbon availability (Ru et al., 2024). These stages should receive high physiological priority because they primarily influence fruit number.

Berry enlargement. This is likely the most important stage for current-season yield response because final berry mass depends heavily on cell expansion and water accumulation. Short periods of water deficit reduced individual berry weight by about 6–15% in susceptible cultivar-stage combinations, with stronger effects later in fruit development (Almutairi et al., 2021). A recent review also identified fruit growth as one of the most drought-sensitive periods, although reported responses varied widely and should not be transferred directly as fixed TelAgri coefficients (Ru et al., 2024). Berry enlargement should therefore receive the highest initial priority for current-season berry mass and yield.

Ripening and post-harvest. During ripening, water limitation may affect final swelling, berry mass, firmness, soluble solids, acidity, ripening rate, and harvest distribution. Responses vary by cultivar and environment (Almutairi et al., 2021), and late irrigation cutoffs have caused significant yield loss in field experiments (Almutairi et al., 2017). Post-harvest stress should be treated separately because it primarily affects vegetative growth, flower-bud development, and next-season reproductive potential (Ru et al., 2024).

StageMain yield component affectedInitial priority
BloomFruit number via floral function and pollinationHigh
Fruit set / early growthFruit number and potential berry sizeHigh
Berry enlargementFinal berry massHighest
RipeningBerry mass, quality, harvest timingHigh
Post-harvestFollowing-season fruit numberHigh for next season
Recommendation: Do not assign fixed numerical yield-loss weights yet. Stage-specific stress indicators should first be calculated separately and calibrated against local yield, berry-weight, and phenology observations.

B2 · Estimating water stress from weather and satellite data

Estimating water stress using weather and satellite data

TelAgri prompt B2

What is the most defensible way to estimate water stress with public weather and satellite data when block-scale ETa is not directly available? Or are there acceptable proxies for ETa that leverage weather and satellite data?

When block-scale actual evapotranspiration (ETa) is unavailable, the most defensible approach is a daily weather-driven root-zone water balance rather than treating satellite-derived ETa as a direct measurement of plant stress. Reference evapotranspiration (ET0) represents atmospheric demand, while rainfall, irrigation, soil water-holding capacity, rooting depth, and canopy development determine whether the crop can meet that demand. FAO-56 represents water limitation using a water-stress coefficient Ks, where Ks = 1 indicates no modeled limitation and Ks < 1 indicates progressively constrained transpiration as root-zone water is depleted (Allen et al., 1998).

FAO-56 adjusted crop evapotranspirationETc,adj=(KsKcb+Ke)ET0

Here, Kcb represents basal crop transpiration and Ke represents soil evaporation. Separating plant transpiration from soil evaporation is useful in blueberry systems because satellite ET may also include exposed soil and inter-row vegetation.

Satellite products should be used mainly as complementary spatial evidence and validation. Landsat-based SSEBop products can identify spatial variation in ET but remain modeled estimates and depend on cloud-free observations (Senay et al., 2026). ECOSTRESS provides thermal and ET information at approximately 70 m resolution and can provide an additional check on modeled water use (Hook & Halverson, 2024). ERA5-Land can provide hourly meteorological information where local weather stations are unavailable, but its approximately 9 km resolution should be interpreted as regional rather than orchard-scale weather (Sabater, 2025).

The largest practical limitation is unknown irrigation. Orchards experiencing identical weather may have very different plant water status because of irrigation management. Where irrigation records are unavailable, the model should use explicit irrigation scenarios or relative water-stress risk classes rather than claim precise plant water deficit.
Recommendation: Use weather and a root-zone water balance as the primary estimate of water limitation. Use satellite ET and thermal information to identify spatial patterns and provide independent checks. Low ETa alone should not be interpreted as blueberry water stress.
← Previous promptB1 · Water stress by growth stage and stage weightsNext prompt →B3 · A practical water-balance / ET-deficit score
B3 · Water-balance / ET-deficit score

Practical water-balance and ET-deficit score

TelAgri prompt B3

Can we build a practical water-balance or ET-deficit score from effective precipitation, reference ET, soil assumptions, and satellite indicators? What are the minimum inputs and largest uncertainties?

A practical score can summarize the difference between potential crop transpiration and modeled actual transpiration during each blueberry growth stage.

Stage-specific water-deficit scoreDs=∑(Tpot−Ta)∑Tpot

Ds = stage-specific water-deficit score; Tpot = potential transpiration without water limitation; Ta = modeled actual transpiration.

A score of 0 indicates no modeled transpiration deficit. Increasing values represent greater cumulative limitation. For example, Ds = 0.30 indicates that modeled transpiration was 30% below potential during that stage; it does not mean that yield was reduced by 30%.

Minimum inputs

InputMinimum information needed
WeatherDaily rainfall and ET0, or weather variables to calculate ET0
SoilAvailable water capacity, rooting depth, drainage assumption
IrrigationTiming and amount, or scenarios if unknown
CropCultivar, canopy status, growth-stage dates
SatelliteQuality-screened canopy or ET observations where available

Largest uncertainties

The largest uncertainties are irrigation, effective rooting depth, soil water-holding capacity, initial root-zone water storage, crop coefficients, and phenological timing. Satellite interpretation may additionally be limited by cloud cover, mixed pixels, and spatial resolution. Uncertain inputs should therefore be represented by plausible ranges or scenarios rather than exact values.

Recommendation: Calculate Ds separately for bloom, fruit set, berry enlargement, and ripening. Also retain maximum depletion and longest consecutive stress period as complementary indicators. Convert water-deficit scores to yield impacts only after validation with observed yield, berry weight, or plant-water-status data.
← Previous promptB2 · Estimating water stress without block-scale ETaNext prompt →B4 · Productivity indicator without double counting
B4 · Productivity indicator without double counting

Integrating fAPAR, water deficit, and chlorophyll information

TelAgri prompt B4

How would you use fapar - previous season, current fapar, effective precipitation, and Cab or chlorophyll information to create a productivity or yield-potential indicator without double-counting stress effects?

A yield-potential indicator can combine canopy development, previous-season canopy condition, water limitation, and chlorophyll information, but each variable should represent a distinct biological process to avoid double counting.

Current-season fAPAR should represent canopy light interception. fAPAR is the fraction of incoming photosynthetically active radiation absorbed by vegetation. Together with incoming PAR, it can be used to estimate absorbed photosynthetically active radiation (APAR):

Absorbed photosynthetically active radiationAPAR=PAR×fAPAR

Conversion of APAR into carbon gain still depends on light-use efficiency and environmental constraints (Running & Zhao, 2019). Current fAPAR should therefore be treated as a canopy-potential indicator rather than a direct measure of photosynthesis or yield.

Previous-season fAPAR may provide useful carryover information about prior canopy condition and activity, but it should not be interpreted as measured carbohydrate reserves, flower-bud number, or future yield. Effective precipitation should enter only through the root-zone water balance and should not then be added again as an independent yield benefit.

Cab/chlorophyll can provide additional information on canopy physiological condition, but lower chlorophyll does not uniquely indicate drought and may also reflect phenology, nutrient status, canopy aging, disease, cultivar differences, or other stresses.

IndicatorProposed biological roleAvoid
Current fAPARCurrent canopy light interceptionDirect photosynthesis or yield
Previous-season fAPARPrior canopy condition / carryoverMeasured bud number or stored carbon
Effective precipitationWater supply through root-zone balanceAdding rainfall again as a yield bonus
Water-deficit score DsModeled water limitationAssuming equal % yield loss
Cab / chlorophyllAdditional canopy-condition informationAssuming every decline represents drought
Productivity / yield-potential indicatorPI=f(APARcurrent,fAPARprevious,1−Ds,Cabanomaly)

PI represents relative productivity or yield potential. Fixed numerical weights should not be assigned initially. Current canopy potential, previous-season condition, stage-specific water deficit, and chlorophyll status should first be evaluated separately and combined only after demonstrating that each contributes independent predictive information to held-out yield observations.

Recommendation: Keep canopy potential, water deficit, previous-season condition, and chlorophyll as separate components until their independent predictive value is demonstrated.

Theme C · TelAgri prompts C1–C4

Satellite indices, weeds and flooding

Answered by Giannis Gallios · G for Geoscience · Satellite evidence for orchard monitoring near Zugdidi · Week 1 technical review · 6 October 2026 · Illustrative imagery + pilot recommendations

Four practical questions: what the indices show, how to examine flooding, when finer imagery helps, and how to turn observations into useful pilot features.

Decision at a glance — start with the field question, then choose the imagery

Sentinel-2 offers a practical public-data starting point for comparing canopy-related signals over time. The same-day PlanetScope comparison shows where ~3 m pixels preserve patterns lost at 10 m. These tests use agricultural demonstration areas near Zugdidi; crop identity, management, and exact orchard blocks have yet to be confirmed by TelAgri.

What we demonstrated

Spatial detail

Same location and date: ~3 m PlanetScope versus 10 m Sentinel-2 RGB.

What we demonstrated

Change through time

Fixed testing locations, NDVI/NDRE/NDMI trajectories, and date-to-date change maps.

What we propose

Orchard pilot

Confirm blocks and crops, reconstruct histories, then test satellite features against field records.

Recommended first step: build a confirmed block registry and assess past image coverage before selecting commercial imagery, index thresholds, or yield-loss equations.

C1 · Measuring indices

Where and when do field conditions change?

TelAgri prompt C1

How should we measure NDRE, NDMI, NDVI, fapar, and Cab for blueberry blocks if we know that they are strongly tied to yield? How do we contextualize those values or make them meaningful?

Reframed: How should NDVI, NDRE, NDMI, fAPAR and Cab be measured and made meaningful for blueberry blocks?

For each confirmed block, extract a quality-controlled seasonal time series, then compare the same location with its own earlier observations and with similar blocks at the same stage. We tested three indices on fixed locations within two illustrative agricultural areas. Their values describe spectral properties of the vegetation–soil mixture; field records explain what caused a change. [1–3]

IndicatorWhat it contributesHow to interpret in the pilot
NDVI
red + near infrared		Green vegetation cover and canopy development.Track seasonal level, decline, and recovery; check bare soil and inter-row vegetation.
NDRE
red edge + near infrared		Chlorophyll-sensitive canopy response.Compare with NDVI; investigate whether it adds useful information in denser canopy.
NDMI
near infrared + shortwave infrared		Moisture-related reflectance of canopy and exposed background.Compare with rain, irrigation, stage, and NDVI; do not equate it with root-zone moisture.
fAPAR
retrieved variable		Fraction of incoming photosynthetically active radiation absorbed by vegetation.Evaluate seasonal light interception alongside canopy development.
Cab
retrieved variable		Estimated leaf chlorophyll content.Evaluate chlorophyll-related change alongside NDRE and field observations.

A consistent extraction workflow

Use surface-reflectance imagery for each confirmed block, screen clouds and shadows, exclude boundary pixels where practical, and extract block summaries together with fixed internal monitoring zones. Retain the acquisition date and valid coverage with every observation, and compare equivalent growth stages and historical conditions. The demonstration TIFFs provide valid-data masks and file checks; future exports should include explicit cloud and shadow quality layers.

IndexFormula used hereSentinel-2 bands
NDVI — Normalized Difference Vegetation Index(NIR − red) / (NIR + red)(B8 − B4) / (B8 + B4)
NDRE — Normalized Difference Red Edge(narrow NIR − red edge) / (narrow NIR + red edge)(B8A − B5) / (B8A + B5)
NDMI — Normalized Difference Moisture Index(NIR − SWIR) / (NIR + SWIR)(B8 − B11) / (B8 + B11)

NIR = near infrared; SWIR = shortwave infrared. NDRE and NDMI use native 20 m bands, even when displayed on a 10 m export grid. A finer display grid does not add independent spatial detail. [1]

During the initial pilot, additional indices and retrieved variables will be evaluated for condition-specific assessment, including canopy development, chlorophyll-related changes, moisture response and exposed-soil effects. Selection will depend on the available bands and whether each feature adds useful information.

What to notice: the three testing locations follow different trajectories, demonstrating why local monitoring can reveal changes hidden by a whole-area average.

See the two date-specific index maps

A common colour scale across dates helps avoid mistaking a different display stretch for change. White areas on 10 May lack valid observations and should remain missing.

How this becomes useful: retain acquisition date, valid coverage, stage, and block metadata with every observation. Once TelAgri provides confirmed blueberry blocks and historical records, compare dates within the same crop stage and measure event-related decline, affected fraction, persistence, and recovery.

C2 · Flood and wetness

Three connected products for the Zugdidi area

TelAgri prompt C2

What satellite-based approach could identify flooding, persistent wetness, or likely anaerobic root-zone conditions? Are there indices that you are comfortable with that can distinguish surface inundation (or even persistent saturation) that can be detected? What are the limitations of that approach?

Reframed: Which satellite approach can identify inundation, persistent wetness, or possible root-zone oxygen stress?

Begin with a regional view that requires little local data, then add event observations and field checks. The approaches answer different questions and can share terrain, water history and rainfall inputs. A UF/IFAS Florida example illustrates how a susceptibility product can be communicated; the Georgian analysis would require its own local inputs and checks. [4–8]

01 · ScreenFlood susceptibilityStack terrain, river proximity, land cover, historical water, rainfall and available soils to rank areas for assessment.
02 · ObserveSurface inundationCompare Sentinel-1 radar before/after an event and corroborate open water with cloud-free Sentinel-2 NDWI/MNDWI.
03 · ConnectPossible plant impactCombine exposure, duration, weather and Orestis’s water-balance/ET work with management and field observations.
ApproachOutput TelAgri could useLocal evidence needed to improve it
SusceptibilityRelative screening map for orchard areas and upstream catchments; prioritizes field checks and drainage questions.Confirmed blocks, drainage features and dated historical flood observations.
Inundation monitoringEvent extent and repeated detections per valid acquisition, with date and confidence.Dated flood/no-flood photos and field observations; river stage and rainfall if available.
Root-zone concernFlag where water exposure may persist and where plant response merits inspection.Drainage, soil/root depth, irrigation, water table or soil moisture, plant observations; oxygen/redox for direct anaerobic evidence.
Practical interpretation: satellites can sometimes detect exposed water; repeat observations cannot show continuous saturation between passes. Under canopy or narrow drainage features, radar and optical imagery may miss water. A susceptibility score is a relative screening layer, not a calibrated flood probability.

A first susceptibility map can be developed from public layers while orchard records are organized. Event monitoring can be tested against known occurrences. An assessment within 1–3 days of a suitable satellite acquisition is an operational target to evaluate, dependent on acquisition and usable coverage. [5–8]

C3 · Weeds and imagery choice

How much detail does the decision require?

TelAgri prompt C3

How could we rate weed control in a blueberry orchard using remote sensing? What is feasible with Sentinel-2 at 10 m, and when would higher-resolution drone or aerial imagery be necessary?

Reframed: What can 10 m Sentinel-2 reveal about weed control, and when does ~3 m PlanetScope or aerial imagery help?

The same-day comparison from 5 June 2026 holds location and acquisition date approximately constant. Both sensors show the landscape; PlanetScope preserves more of the narrow and mixed features. At 10 m a nominal pixel covers 100 m², while at 3 m it covers 9 m². This visual test demonstrates spatial detail, not validated weed detection. [1–2]

Spatial resolution and band choice both matter

Band / signalSuperDove 8-band (~3 m)Sentinel-2 native pixelsWhy it matters
Blue, green, redAvailable10 mVisible colour and reflectance; red contributes to NDVI.
Near infrared (NIR)AvailableB8 10 m; B8A 20 mSupports vegetation indices with red and red-edge.
Red edgeOne bandB5, B6, B7 at 20 mSupports NDRE/chlorophyll-sensitive indicators.
Shortwave infrared (SWIR)Not availableB11, B12 at 20 mRequired for standard NDMI and MNDWI.
Extra visible bandsCoastal blue, green I, yellowDifferent band setMay help discrimination, subject to local testing.
Proposed weed-control measurement: where the imagery separates management zones, estimate unwanted vegetation as a percentage of the valid observed area within crop rows or managed inter-rows, then track recurrence between management operations. Label deliberate grass cover separately. Use Sentinel-2 for broad vegetation context, test Planet where zones span multiple pixels, and use drone or aerial imagery for individual rows and small patches.

Weed-control concept: first delineate crop rows, inter-rows and block edges. Measure unwanted green cover, its persistence and spatial extent in the inter-row or crop row zone, while distinguishing deliberate ground cover. Sentinel-2 can provide broad block-level context. Test 3 m imagery where the target zones span multiple pixels; use drone or aerial imagery and field ratings for narrow rows, small patches and validation. The eight-band SuperDove product used here supports NDVI and NDRE, while standard NDMI requires Sentinel-2’s SWIR. [1–2]

C4 · Initial features

Translate observations into testable condition scores

TelAgri prompt C4

In your experience with modeling, what are typically the most reliable reliable satellite feature set for a first yield-loss model, and how should each feature be converted into a simple deterministic score?

Reframed: Which satellite features belong in an initial model, and how could they become transparent deterministic scores?

Begin with a few complementary feature groups rather than treating every index as an independent yield driver. For a confirmed orchard block and growth-stage window, compare observed values to a matched reference: the same block in comparable past seasons or similar blocks of the same cultivar and age where records support that comparison.

Feature groupSimple first measureWhat the score expresses
Canopy developmentStage-specific NDVI level and changeHow far vegetation development departs from its reference.
Chlorophyll-sensitive responseNDRE departure among observations with similar NDVI and growth stageWhether red-edge behavior adds evidence beyond NDVI.
Moisture-related responseNDMI anomaly + weather/water-balance contextWhether moisture-related spectral condition warrants investigation.
Event and spatial footprintMagnitude × duration; affected fraction; recoveryHow extensive and persistent the change is.
Initial condition score: departure severity × affected fraction × persistence gives a relative inspection priority. Keep acquisition quality and observation age alongside the result. Pablo and Orestis can later review crop-stage sensitivity; field records will support threshold calibration.

A worked example

For a moisture-related condition, compare NDMI with a reference range for the same growth stage. Define departure severity from 0 to 1 using agreed bounds, measure the affected fraction from 0 to 1, and define persistence as the fraction of usable observations showing the departure within a specified event window.

Illustrative inputValue
Departure severity0.60
Affected fraction of valid block area0.40
Persistence: departure in 3 of 4 usable observations0.75
Inspection priority: 100 × 0.60 × 0.40 × 0.7518 / 100

The values illustrate the calculation; thresholds will be selected during the pilot. Missing acquisitions are excluded from the persistence denominator. Observation dates describe recurrence at satellite visits, rather than continuous duration. Apply the same structure to a specified NDVI or NDRE departure, retaining separate condition scores so correlated indices do not create repeated penalties. Yield-loss percentages require a later relationship with field yield records.

The comparison with TelAgri’s eventual yield-deviation labels should include simple baselines, independent farm/season evaluation, missingness, and subgroup checks. Features or indices that add little information can then be removed.

Appendix · Theme C supplementary package

Notebooks and data accompanying the satellite review

Package README — Telagri Satellite Review — 6 October 2026 · Giannis Gallios

Open satellite_report.html in a modern browser. It contains all images, styles, and navigation locally. Click a figure to enlarge it. An internet connection is only needed if you choose to open external reference links.

The data/ folder contains observations, acquisition quality control, and the fixed testing-location coordinates used for the illustrative figures.

The notebooks/ folder is an optional technical appendix. To rerun either notebook, create a data/ directory beside that notebook and add the original imagery TIFFs. Required naming/configuration is documented in each notebook:

  • Planet_vs_Sentinel_spatial_comparison.ipynb needs the 8-band SuperDove surface-reflectance TIFF and the 5 June Sentinel-2 multiband TIFF.
  • Sentinel2_index_time_series.ipynb needs S2_YYYY-MM-DD_13bands.tif files.

The spatial notebook uses a common 0.02–0.30 display range and original raster grids. Set each reflectance divisor to match the supplied export. The time-series notebook uses the selected manual locations shown in the report. The TIFFs are not included. The report itself requires none of these files.

The two illustrative agricultural areas have not been confirmed as TelAgri blueberry blocks. Field geometry, crop identity, management and records are needed for orchard-specific interpretation.

From our team to TelAgri

Questions that decide what we build

Our answers to the twelve prompts depend on how TelAgri’s current model and data are set up. These six questions are what we need answered next.

  1. 1

    What does the model output today — stage, yield, loss or risk — and for which unit: block, pixel or farm?

  2. 2

    Which cultivars are in each block, and which matter most?

  3. 3

    Is weather hourly or daily, and from stations or gridded products?

  4. 4

    Do any bloom dates, frost-damage notes or block yield histories exist?

  5. 5

    How are stresses combined now: summed percentages or sequential states?

  6. 6

    Which part of the current model does Telagri trust least?
